title: Origin of Earth's oceans
summary: When Earth's oceans formed is debated. A University of Wisconsin study of a Jack Hills zircon finds that Earth's crust had formed at least 4.4 billion years ago, supporting a cool early Earth with liquid water and a hydrosphere before 4.3 billion years ago. NOAA dates the ocean's filling to about 3.8 billion years ago, when water vapour released from the planet's interior condensed into rain.

uncertainty.note: Jack Hills detrital zircon W74/2-36 yields a U-Pb age of 4,404 ± 8 Ma with elevated oxygen isotopes indicating low-temperature surface water interaction (Valley et al.); marine sedimentary rocks in the Isua supracrustal belt confirm widespread oceans by 3.8 Ga.

as_recorded.calendar: U-Pb zircon geochronology and atom-probe tomography
as_recorded.value: habitable to life about 4.4 billion years ago
At this time, about 3.8 billion years ago, the water condensed into rain which filled the basins that we now know as our world ocean.

where.modern_name: No single place; stand-in pin at Jack Hills, Western Australia
where.historical_name: Hadean Earth; early oceans condensing across primordial crust

paleo.not_applicable: Predates plate tectonic reconstructions; global planetary process.

importance.justification: The accumulation of Earth's oceans established the global hydrosphere, regulating planetary climate and providing the essential aqueous medium for the origin and diversification of life.

related.because: Planetary accretion and interior differentiation drove degassing of water vapor into the cooling atmosphere.
The presence of stable liquid oceans provided the necessary chemical soup and hydrothermal environments for the origin of life.
